Take the offline multilingual avatar I built for Mercedes-Benz Germany. It had to work without a cloud round trip. No token price, however low, would have changed that requirement. The same was true of a real-time detection system for a defence deployment. The data was never going to leave the building.

Cheap frontier intelligence is great news for a specific class of work: batch jobs, coding agents, back-office automation where the data can leave. For that, a fifth of the price is a gift, and I would re-run your cost model this week.

But notice what a price cut really tells you. The vendor sets the price. Last month it was Astra at five times the cost. Next quarter it could be something else. Prices fall when the vendor decides, and they can change in either direction. A dependency you do not control is a dependency whether it is expensive or cheap.

Here is how I would use this news in practice.

First, benchmark Sol against your real workload, not the launch charts. Near-Astra on public benchmarks says little about your documents, your languages, your edge cases. I have seen hallucination behave very differently in Indic languages than the headline numbers suggest, and that is exactly the kind of gap a vendor chart will not show you.

Second, put a thin abstraction between your product and the model. If switching models takes a week of rewrites, you are not saving money, you are renting a lock-in at a discount.

Third, keep a smaller model you control in the loop for the work that must stay local. Retrieval, classification, redaction, routing. Most of a production pipeline does not need frontier reasoning. It needs to be fast, private and predictable.

Fourth, log what each call is worth. A cheaper model invites you to call it more. Without per-task cost and quality tracking, a 5x price cut turns into a 5x increase in usage and the same bill.

There is a pattern here I keep seeing. Every time a price drops, the conversation becomes about spending less. The better question is what you can now build that you could not justify before, and which parts of it should never depend on someone else's servers at all.

My bias is well known: models should run where the data is. On-device, offline, under your control. Cheaper cloud inference does not weaken that argument. It sharpens it, because now the only reason left to send data out is that you actually need to.

Takeaway: use the discount, but design as if the price, the model and the endpoint can all change tomorrow. Because they can.

title: Robots now think with a cloud model. Most factory floors can't depend on that.
body:
Hot take: the hard part of putting a foundation model in a robot is not the model. It is the network cable you quietly assume is there.

Boston Dynamics and Google DeepMind have partnered to bring Gemini Robotics models to Atlas and Spot. It was announced at CES 2026, and the Spot inspection platform has since picked up Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6, a reasoning model DeepMind released in April. Industrial testing is aimed first at automotive factories.

I think this is a real step. A robot that can interpret sensor data and plan around irregular objects is far more useful than one running scripted routines. But the interesting question is where that reasoning runs.

I have shipped enough systems into defence, automotive and education settings to know what deployment looks like. The demo has fast internet and a friendly room. The real site has a locked-down network, a security team, and a hard rule about what data leaves the building.

An inspection robot sees things the plant owner may not want to leave the premises. Layouts, equipment, process details. A defence deployment I worked on made this very concrete: if the system needs a round trip to someone else's servers to decide what to do next, it is not a system you control.

Latency matters too. A model that reasons about physical space has to answer inside the control loop's tolerance, not inside a cloud request's. When the link drops, the robot should degrade gracefully, not freeze mid-task.

This is why I keep arguing that models should run where the data is. For an offline multilingual avatar I built for an automotive client in Germany, offline was not a feature. It was the requirement that made the product shippable.

So when I read robotics announcements, I ask three questions.

First, which parts of the stack run on the device and which call out? A high-level reasoning model and a low-level controller have very different tolerances, and the split should be explicit.

Second, what happens when connectivity is gone? The answer should be a defined fallback behaviour, tested, not a hope.

Third, what leaves the premises, and who can audit it? If the vendor cannot answer in one paragraph, the pilot is not ready for a real plant.

None of this is a criticism of the partnership. Pairing strong hardware with strong models is the right direction. Factory pilots will force exactly these questions, and the teams that answer them early will be the ones that scale.

I also expect on-device and edge-sized robot models to matter more over the next year, precisely because of these constraints. The vendor that makes the reasoning layer run locally, with a cloud option rather than a cloud dependency, will have the easier enterprise conversation.

Hardware cycles are slow and software cycles are fast. A robot bought today will outlive several model versions, so the architecture has to let the model change without reworking the safety case.

If you are evaluating an embodied AI pilot, write down the offline behaviour before you sign anything.

Takeaway: a robot that only thinks when the network does is a remote control with extra steps.

title: Exploits now arrive in under a day. Your patch cycle still runs on weeks.
body:
Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report has one number that should change how you plan: the median time from a vulnerability being discovered in the wild to it being weaponized is now well under 24 hours.

Your patch cycle is probably measured in weeks. That gap is the story.

The same report says phishing was the way in for 23% of the intrusions Microsoft's incident responders investigated between July 2025 and June 2026. A year earlier it was 7%. The explanation is simple. AI lets an attacker personalize every message, so spear phishing stops being a craft and becomes a mass operation.

I have spent years building AI systems for places where a failure is not a bad demo, including a defence deployment where the threat model was part of the spec on day one. The lesson from that work is blunt: defenders who treat AI as a feature to bolt on will lose to attackers who treat it as infrastructure.

Here is what I think follows from the report.

First, your architecture has to assume the exploit window is hours. If the only thing between a disclosed bug and your data is a weekly patch meeting, you have already lost. Segmentation, least privilege and fast rollback matter more than any detection model.

Second, the AI you deploy is attack surface too. Every model endpoint, every agent with tool access, every RAG pipeline that ingests untrusted documents is a new way in. I see teams wire an agent to internal systems with broad credentials because it made the demo work. That is the same mistake as an admin account with a shared password, just with better marketing.

Third, where the model runs is a security decision. A model that sends your documents to a third-party cloud has extended your perimeter to someone else's logging policy. My bias has always been that models should run where the data is: on-device, offline, under your control. The Microsoft numbers make that bias look less like a preference and more like basic hygiene.

Fourth, be careful with vendor claims about AI defenders. This week Google launched a new model to trusted cyber defenders first, and the headline claims are about autonomously finding and fixing vulnerabilities. Maybe. But reporting says no independent lab has reproduced the published scores yet. I would treat that as a promising lead, not a control. Run your own evaluation on your own code before you let anything patch production.

None of this means panic. It means the boring work just got urgent. Inventory what you expose. Shorten the time from advisory to patch. Give agents the narrowest credentials that let them do the job. Train people against phishing that no longer has typos.

And if you are building AI for a regulated or sensitive environment, write down where each model runs and what data it can touch. If that page is hard to write, that is your real finding.

The attackers already treat AI as infrastructure. The takeaway: your security plan should too, and it should be measured in hours, not weeks.

title: A deepfake detector that runs on light is a hardware story, not a model story.
body:
UCLA researchers just showed a chip that screens 15 video streams for deepfakes in a single optical pass, at 97.79% accuracy on the Celeb-DF benchmark. At 18 streams it still holds 96.13%. The paper is in eLight, and the preprint is on arXiv.

The headline number is not what caught my attention. The architecture did.

Most detection pipelines I see are digital and sequential. A video goes in, frames get decoded, a model scores them, the next video waits. Throughput is a GPU bill. Here, part of the computation happens as light propagates through the optics, so many streams are evaluated at the same time instead of queued.

That matters because the deepfake problem is a volume problem. Generating a fake is cheap and getting cheaper. Checking one costs real compute, and you have to check all of them, including the ones that turn out to be real.

I have spent years building real-time detection systems, including a drone threat detection system for Indian Army and Police use. The lesson from that kind of work is that accuracy is the easy part to talk about and latency and power are the hard part to ship. A model that is great on a benchmark but needs a rack of GPUs is not deployable where the data is generated.

So an approach that cuts energy per stream and scales by multiplexing is the right direction. It is the same bias I keep coming back to: inference should run close to the data, offline if possible, under your control. Sending every suspect video to a cloud API to be scored is a privacy problem as well as a cost problem.

Now the caveats, because there are real ones.

First, this is a research result on a benchmark. Celeb-DF is a known dataset. Detectors that look excellent on a fixed benchmark routinely lose a lot of accuracy on fakes from a generator they have not seen. I would want to see out-of-distribution numbers before trusting any figure here.

Second, a chip is not a product. Optical hardware has to be fabricated, calibrated, integrated with decoders and fed video at line rate. Those integration steps are where research prototypes usually spend years.

Third, the reports mention resistance to attacks as an advantage. That is plausible, since a physical optical stage is harder to probe with gradient-based adversarial methods than a software model you can query. But harder is not immune, and I would treat that claim as something to test, not assume.

Still, the shift is worth noticing. For the last few years the conversation about AI has been almost entirely about models: bigger, cheaper, better. This result is a reminder that the next real gains in some workloads may come from changing what the computation physically runs on.

If you are building detection or moderation pipelines today, there are two practical things to do. Measure your cost per stream, not just your accuracy. And test your detector on generators it was not trained on, because that is the only number that will predict what happens in production.

Takeaway: deepfake detection will be won on throughput, energy and generalisation, and the benchmark score is only the least interesting of the three.

title: A 125B model now runs on a gaming GPU. Whether it's good enough is the real question.
body:
A 125-billion-parameter model running on a single gaming GPU with about 12GB of VRAM. That was this week's headline, and it deserves a closer read than the headline gets.

The project is Strata, an open-source inference engine, and the model is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 24,576 small experts, and each token only touches 10 of them. Strata keeps the hot experts cached in VRAM, holds the full set in system RAM, and lets the CPU handle whatever missed the cache.

The reported speeds are around 94 tokens per second on an RTX 5070 and around 60 on an RX 9070 XT, at aggressive 2-bit quantization. Those are the project's own numbers, so treat them as a ceiling, not a promise.

Here is why I care. My bias has not changed in years: models should run where the data is. On-device, offline, under your control.

I have shipped systems where the network was not an option. An offline multilingual avatar had to work with no connection at all. A defence deployment could not send a single frame off the device. In those projects, the model was never the hard part. The hard part was fitting a capable model into hardware someone had already bought.

Mixture-of-experts changes that arithmetic. Total parameters stop being the number that sets your hardware floor. Active parameters and memory traffic do.

But I want to be careful, because this is where demos and products part ways.

First, 2-bit quantization is not free. Quality loss shows up unevenly. It tends to hide in long-tail behaviour, in rare languages, and in structured output. If you work with Indic languages, as I do in my hallucination research, you learn quickly that an average benchmark score says very little about the languages at the edges. Measure on your own data.

Second, expert offloading makes latency uneven. When the experts a prompt needs are not in the cache, the CPU path takes over and speed drops. Throughput on a clean benchmark prompt is not throughput on your traffic. Look at the worst case, not the median.

Third, a one-click installer is not a deployment. Production means pinned versions, health checks, drift monitoring, and a rollback plan. An engine that is at an early version number needs a wrapper of discipline around it.

None of this makes Strata less interesting. It makes it correctly interesting. For a prototype, a private internal assistant, or a data-sensitive workflow where cloud APIs are ruled out, the barrier just dropped to a machine many teams already own.

It also puts pressure on a habit I see everywhere: defaulting to a hosted API because local was too hard. Local is getting less hard every month. The honest question is now whether your use case needs the cloud, not whether you can avoid it.

If I were evaluating this today, I would do three things. Run my own evaluation set at the quantization level I plan to ship. Test with realistic concurrent traffic, not a single prompt. And write down what happens when the engine fails.

The takeaway: the hardware excuse for sending your data to someone else's server is getting thinner. Your evaluation set is the only thing that tells you whether the local model is good enough.

title: NIST just published an AI evaluation framework, and its best feature is no checklist.
body:
NIST just published a framework for evaluating AI systems, and the best thing about it is what it refuses to give you: a checklist.

The draft is NIST AI 200-2, called the TEVV-Athlon. Public comment closed on October 6. It describes a four-stage method for building a customized assessment around your own test, evaluation, verification and validation goals. NIST says plainly that no single list of tests works for every system, because the systems and their risks vary too much.

I think that is the right call, and it matches what I have seen in production.

Take a real-time detection system I worked on for a defence deployment. A headline precision number looked great in the lab. But the number that mattered in the field was different: what happens at dusk, with a degraded camera feed, when an operator has four seconds to decide. No generic benchmark measures that. We had to design the evaluation around the mission, not the model.

The same is true for LLM products. A leaderboard score tells you how a model does on someone else's questions. It says nothing about your documents, your users, or your failure costs.

When I wrote about hallucination in Indic languages, this was the core problem. A model can look fine on English benchmarks and quietly fall apart in Hindi or Kannada. If your evaluation was never built for your language and your domain, you will not see it until a user does.

That is why the framing in this draft matters. The TEVV-Athlon treats evaluation as a set of events and tools that generate data on specific measurement concepts. In plain terms: decide what you are trying to measure first, then pick the tests. Most teams do it backwards. They pick a benchmark because it is popular, then work out what it means.

Here is how I would use it, even before it is final:

First, write down the three failures that would actually hurt. Not "accuracy". Real failures: a wrong answer a customer acts on, a refusal that blocks a workflow, a silent drift after a model update.

Second, build a test for each one from your own data. Small is fine. Fifty good cases that reflect your reality beat five thousand generic ones.

Third, run them on every change. Model swap, prompt edit, retrieval tweak. Evaluation is not a launch gate, it is a regression suite.

Fourth, keep it local. If your evaluation data is sensitive, which it often is in defence, automotive and education, it should be runnable offline, on your own machines. I have always believed models should run where the data is, and your tests should too.

One more point. A framework that is not a compliance checklist is harder to adopt. A checklist lets you tick boxes and feel safe. A method makes you think, and thinking costs time. Expect some organizations to wish NIST had just handed them a list.

I would still take the harder version. A checklist gives you the comfort of a pass. A custom evaluation gives you the truth about your own system, and that is the only thing that survives contact with production.

This is a draft, and details may change before it is final. But the direction is correct, and you do not need to wait for the final version to start.

Takeaway: stop asking which benchmark your model won. Ask which failure you can no longer afford, and build the test that catches it.

title: Open-weight isn't open until you can download it: what to test on Reflection's Beam
body:
Hot take: an open-weight model is not open until you can download it, run it, and audit it.

On Monday, Reflection AI unveiled Beam, its first model. TechCrunch and Fortune both covered it. It is a text-only mixture-of-experts model, reported at 501 billion total parameters with 23 billion active, and a 1 million token context window. Reflection says the weights and full technical details will arrive this month.

Notice the tense. Will arrive. As I write this, the announcement is real and the weights are a promise.

The performance claims are Reflection's own. The company says Beam matches Z.ai's GLM-5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks and needs three to four times less inference compute than rival open models. Neither outlet independently verified that. I am not saying it is wrong. I am saying a vendor benchmark is a hypothesis, not a result.

Here is why I care. My bias has always been that models should run where the data is: on-device, offline, under your control. In the defence work I have been part of, "we call an API" was never an acceptable answer. The data could not leave the building, and neither could the model's behaviour be a mystery.

That is the real value of open weights, and it has little to do with ideology. It is about three practical things.

First, you can pin a version. A hosted model can change under you on a Tuesday. A file on your disk cannot.

Second, you can inspect it. I have spent a lot of time on interpretability and on hallucination in Indic languages. You cannot study what you cannot load. Closed endpoints give you outputs, and outputs alone are a thin basis for a safety argument.

Third, you can put it next to the data. Offline deployments, like the multilingual avatar work I did for an automotive client, only work if the model fits inside the environment you control.

Now the engineering reality check on a 501B-parameter model. Only 23 billion parameters are active per token, which helps compute. It does not help memory. All the experts still have to live somewhere. Active parameters set your speed. Total parameters set your hardware bill. People confuse the two constantly.

So if Beam ships as promised, here is what I would test before believing any headline number:

1. Your own evaluation set, not the vendor's. Take a few hundred real tasks from your domain and score them blind.

2. Long context under load. A 1 million token window on paper and a 1 million token window that stays accurate are different products.

3. Quantised behaviour. Most teams will not run full precision. Measure what you lose at 8-bit and 4-bit, especially on non-English text.

4. The licence. The coverage I read does not state the terms. "Open-weight" can mean anything from Apache-style freedom to heavy restrictions. Read it before you build on it.

5. Cost per correct answer, not cost per token. A cheaper token that needs more retries is not cheaper.

There is a broader point here too. A strong Western open-weight option matters for anyone who wants choice outside a handful of hosted providers. Competition on open weights pushes everyone toward models you can actually own. That is good for builders, whoever wins.

But I will believe it when I have the weights on my own machine and my own test set has run against them.

Takeaway: judge an open model by what you can download and verify, not by what was announced.

title: Haiku 5.5 is 75% cheaper. The real win is that the small model finally gets a job.
body:
Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, and the headline is price. Anthropic says it costs around 75% less than Haiku 4.5 for most work: $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output for prompts up to 100K tokens, rising to $0.50 and $2.50 beyond that. Anthropic and the trade coverage agree on those numbers.

Everyone will quote the discount. I care more about how it is positioned: as a subagent model, sitting under bigger models that plan and decide.

That is the architecture I keep ending up with in production. One capable model makes the plan. Many small, fast, cheap workers do the narrow jobs: classify this, extract that, check this output against a rule. The big model is the manager. The small model is the workforce.

Most teams I see do the opposite. They send every step through the biggest model because it was the easiest thing to wire up in week one. Then the bill arrives and they call it an inference cost problem. It is a design problem.

Here is the test I use. For each step in an agent loop, ask whether a wrong answer is cheap to detect. If a deterministic check can catch the failure, the step does not need your best model. It needs a fast one and a verifier.

Extraction is the clean example. Pull a field out of a document, validate it against a schema, retry on failure. A small model with a validator beats a large model with no validator, and it does it faster.

Hallucination checks work the same way. I have built tooling around detecting unsupported claims, and the lesson was always that verification is a narrower task than generation. Narrow tasks are where small models earn their place.

Now the caveat. A 75% cheaper API model is still an API model. You are still sending data out, still depending on someone else's availability, and still exposed to their next pricing change. Cheap rented intelligence is better than expensive rented intelligence, but it is still rented.

My bias has not changed: models should run where the data is. In the defence and automotive deployments I have worked on, the question was never only cost per token. It was whether the data was allowed to leave the building at all. For those jobs, the subagent pattern is exactly what lets you swap the small worker for an on-device model and keep the planner wherever policy allows.

That is the practical advice. Design your agents so the worker tier is replaceable. Define each worker by its input, its output schema, and its check. Then it does not matter whether it is Haiku today, an open-weight model next quarter, or something running offline on your own hardware.

Also watch the 100K token threshold. Anthropic says prompts up to that size make up around 90% of requests to the previous Haiku, which is why the headline discount applies to most people. If your workload stuffs huge contexts into every call, your real savings are smaller than the headline. Measure your own prompt-length distribution before you plan a budget around a press release.

Two things to do this week. First, list every step in your agent pipeline and mark which ones have a cheap verifier. Second, route those steps to the smallest model that passes the verifier at your required accuracy, and measure it on your own data, not a leaderboard.

Takeaway: a cheaper small model does not fix a bad architecture. It rewards a good one.

title: Hot take: 722 AI-written math papers prove nothing until someone can rerun them
body:
Hot take: 722 AI-written math papers prove nothing until someone can rerun the process that wrote them.

On October 6, OpenAI put 722 math manuscripts on GitHub, all produced by a model it has not released. Multiple outlets report that nearly all of them came from a single prompt given to a single agent. Only some of the papers ship with Lean formal proofs. The prompts, the model name and the per-problem compute are not public.

I want to be fair here. Publishing the manuscripts openly under a permissive licence is a real contribution, and mathematicians can now go and judge them. That is more than most labs do. But the interesting part isn't the volume. It's what the release does and does not let you check.

I work with formal verification and I publish open-access research with permanent DOIs, so I have a bias. A result is only as good as your ability to reproduce it. A Lean proof is the gold standard because a machine checks every step and you don't have to trust the author, human or otherwise. For the papers that have one, the argument is over. The proof compiles or it doesn't.

For the papers without one, you are back to peer review. And peer review at this scale is a human bottleneck. Seven hundred manuscripts is years of referee time, and referees are volunteers. Generation is now cheap and verification is still expensive. That asymmetry is the whole story.

I have seen the same pattern in production AI work. In a defence deployment I worked on, generating candidate detections was never the hard part. Deciding which ones were safe to act on was. We spent most of our engineering effort on the checking layer, not the model. A system that produces output faster than you can validate it is not a productivity gain. It is a queue.

The single-prompt claim is the other thing I would not take on faith. If one prompt really produced most of this, that is remarkable, and it is also unfalsifiable today. Nobody outside the lab can rerun it, because the model is unreleased and the prompt is private. A claim you cannot rerun is a press release with a bibliography.

This is also why I keep pushing for models that run where the data is, under your control. When the model, the prompt and the compute are all in someone else's hands, "trust us" is your only audit trail. When you control the stack, you can pin the version, log the inputs and reproduce the output next month. That is not a philosophical preference. It is what makes a result defensible.

So what should a lab do when it releases machine-generated research? Four things, none of them exotic.

First, ship a formal proof wherever the domain allows one, and say plainly which results lack it. Second, publish the prompt and the harness, even if the weights stay private. Third, record the model version and the compute budget so others can estimate cost per result. Fourth, flag unverified claims in the repository itself, not in a footnote. OpenAI's README does warn that some unformalized results may have problems, which is the right instinct. It needs to go further.

If you are building anything where an AI produces claims that people will rely on, copy this lesson for your own system. Treat the verifier as the product and the generator as a component. Budget more for checking than for creating, and make every output traceable to an input you can replay.

The volume of AI-generated work will keep climbing. The scarce resource is not ideas or even proofs. It is trust you can audit.

Takeaway: if you can't rerun it, you can't rely on it, no matter how many pages it has.

title: Mistral's 1T-parameter Large 4 means nothing until the open weights actually ship
body:
Mistral just previewed a 1-trillion-parameter model and promised the weights by the end of October. I will believe the second half when I can download it.

Here is what is reported. Mistral opened a public preview of Large 4 around October 6, through its own studio and API. Coverage describes it as a natively multimodal model at roughly a trillion parameters, with a final release and open weights planned before the month ends. Outlets disagree on details like active parameter counts and GPU numbers, so I am ignoring those.

The promise matters more than the size. A preview behind an API is a product demo. Weights on disk are a different thing entirely.

I have spent years building systems that have to run where the data lives. In a defence deployment I worked on, nothing was allowed to leave the network. In an automotive project, the avatar had to work offline, in multiple languages, with no cloud round trip. For those jobs, an API-only frontier model is not a candidate, however good its benchmarks are.

So when a lab says "open weights," my first question is not about the leaderboard. It is about what I can actually do with the artifact.

Can I run it inside an air-gapped environment? Is the license something a legal team can sign off on? Can I quantize it and measure what breaks? Can I fine-tune it on my own data without asking permission?

A trillion parameters also changes who counts as "able to self-host." Almost no team I work with has the hardware to serve this model at useful latency. Open weights at this scale are a gift to cloud providers and a handful of well-funded labs first. Everyone else gets it through a distillation, a smaller sibling, or a hosted endpoint run by someone else.

That is not a complaint. It is just the honest shape of the thing. The real value for most practitioners will be what the community builds from it: smaller distilled models, quantized variants, and domain fine-tunes that fit on hardware you control.

There is also a verification problem. A preview is a moving target. Behaviour, safety tuning, and tokenizer details can all change before the final weights land. If you are planning a production system around this model, do not benchmark the preview and call it done. Re-run your own evaluation on the released weights, on your own data, including the languages you care about. Multilingual claims in particular deserve suspicion. I have seen how quickly hallucination rates climb in Indic languages when a model was tuned mostly on English.

My practical advice for the next three weeks:

Write your evaluation set now, before the weights ship. Include your hardest real cases, not the polished ones.

Decide in advance what "good enough" means for your use case, including latency and memory budget on the hardware you actually own.

Plan for the smaller derivatives, not the flagship. That is where on-device and on-premise work will actually happen.

And read the license before you read the benchmark table.

The takeaway: open weights are a deliverable, not an announcement. Judge the release by what you can run, audit, and change on your own machines, and ignore the headline parameter count.

title: The EU AI Act disclosure rule is live, and it is an architecture problem, not a legal one
body:
The EU AI Act's chatbot disclosure rule has been live since 2 August. Most teams I talk to still treat it as a legal problem. It is an architecture problem.

Article 50 says that if your system talks to people, they must be told they are dealing with an AI, unless that is obvious. If it generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, the output has to be marked in a machine-readable way. Deployers publishing deepfakes must disclose them. Law firms tracking this, including Cooley, Sidley and Stibbe, describe the same four areas and the same 2 August date. Fines can reach 15 million euros or 3% of worldwide turnover.

There is one wrinkle. Under the Digital Omnibus, the machine-readable marking duty in Article 50(2) only bites from 2 December 2026 for systems already on the market before 2 August. Newer systems have no grace period.

Here is why I call it an architecture problem. Disclosure is easy when you own the whole pipeline. It gets hard when generated text passes through three services, a cache and a translation layer before a user sees it. Where does the marker live? Who adds it? What happens when someone copies the text out?

I have shipped enough multilingual, customer-facing AI systems to know how this goes. The disclosure banner gets added to the UI at the end, and the first time the output is consumed by something other than the UI, the banner is gone.

So my advice is to treat provenance as a first-class field, not a decoration. Every generation gets a record: which model, which version, which pipeline, when. The marker is attached at the point of generation, not at the point of display. Anything downstream that transforms the content has to carry the marker forward or fail loudly.

This is also where my bias shows. Systems that run on-device or offline, under your control, are far easier to make compliant. You know exactly what model produced the output because you deployed it. You are not trusting an upstream API to keep its behaviour, its watermarking or its versioning stable. In an offline deployment I worked on, the avatar was disclosed as an AI from the first frame, because we owned every layer between the model and the screen.

With a hosted API chain you inherit whatever your vendors decide. If a vendor changes how outputs are marked, your compliance posture changes without a deploy on your side.

Three things I would do this quarter if I were running an LLM product that touches EU users.

First, inventory every surface where model output reaches a person or leaves your system: UI, email, PDF export, API response, webhook. Disclosure has to survive each one.

Second, log generation provenance at the source. If a regulator or a customer asks what produced a given piece of content, you should answer from a database query, not from memory.

Third, test it adversarially. Copy the output, paste it elsewhere, run it through your own translation step, and check whether the disclosure and the marker are still there. If they are not, you have found your gap before someone else does.

Also, read the Commission's guidelines and the voluntary code of practice on AI-generated content transparency rather than relying on summaries, mine included. Law-firm notes are good for orientation, but the binding text is Regulation 2024/1689.

I have seen too many compliance efforts stall because they were handed to legal alone. Legal can tell you what must be true. Only engineering can make it true at every hop.

The takeaway: compliance with Article 50 is a property of your pipeline, so design the pipeline to carry it.

title: Reflection's Beam has 23B active parameters. Your GPU bill will be set by the other 478B.
body:
Everyone will repeat the small number. Reflection AI's first open-weight model, Beam, was announced on October 5 as a sparse Mixture-of-Experts system with 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active per token. The 23B is the headline. It is not the number that decides what you pay.

Here is what is reported. Axios broke the story on October 4 that Reflection, an Nvidia-backed startup founded by former Google DeepMind researchers, was close to releasing its first open-weight model. Follow-up coverage describes Beam as text-only and pitched as a lower-cost alternative to the leading Chinese open-weight models. The weights and technical details are promised this month, and at least one source points to an Apache 2.0 license. As of the coverage I could find, the weights were not yet public. Treat everything below as conditional on them shipping.

Now the engineering point. Active parameters tell you how much compute a single token costs. They say nothing about how much memory you need to hold the model. In an MoE, every expert has to be resident, or you pay a latency penalty fetching it. A 501B model needs the memory footprint of a 501B model, even if each token only touches a slice.

At 8-bit that is roughly 500 GB of weights before you count the KV cache. Even at 4-bit you are well past a single GPU. So the cheap-to-run story is true for throughput on a cluster that is already provisioned. It is not true for the team that wants to run this on one box.

I have watched this confusion in production. When I scope a deployment, the first question is never tokens per second. It is where the weights live and who controls that machine. In the defence and automotive work I have been part of, the model had to run offline, inside a boundary the customer owned. A model you can only serve from a multi-node cluster is a hosted service with extra steps.

That is why I keep a simple checklist for any open-weight release:

1. Total parameters, not active, against the memory I actually have.
2. A license my legal team can sign without a phone call.
3. Weights I can download and run air-gapped.
4. Quantized variants, ideally published by the lab itself.
5. An evaluation I can rerun on my own data.

Beam may clear some of these. We will know when the files are public. Until then it is an announcement, and I do not build on announcements.

None of this makes the release unimportant. A credible US-origin open-weight option matters for teams who cannot or will not depend on Chinese-origin weights, and competition on price helps everyone. If the license is as permissive as reported, it widens the choices for regulated buyers.

But for most of the systems I have shipped, the right answer was a much smaller model, specialised, quantized, and sitting next to the data. The most useful open-weight models are the ones that fit on hardware you already own.

My takeaway: when a lab quotes active parameters, ask for the memory requirement. That is the number your infrastructure budget actually answers to.

title: Utah's AI prescription pilot hinges on one number nobody has published: how often it asks a human
body:
Hot take: the interesting part of Utah's AI prescription pilot is not that an AI renews prescriptions. It is that nobody can yet say how often it hands a case back to a human.

Here is what is reported. Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, working through its regulatory sandbox, signed a mitigation agreement with a company called Doctronic. The pilot lets an AI system renew existing prescriptions for roughly 190 commonly prescribed maintenance drugs, in 30, 60 or 90 day amounts. Controlled substances are excluded. It does not write new prescriptions. Early on, physicians review the renewals.

The pushback is also reported. Utah's medical licensing board and the AMA have objected, arguing that a renewal is not a routine checkbox, especially for drugs where a patient's condition changes. The state has not halted the pilot.

I have no standing to say whether this is good medicine. I do have standing on the engineering, because I have spent years shipping systems where a wrong answer has a real cost, including a defence deployment where false alarms were as damaging as misses.

So here is how I read this pilot as a systems person.

First, the model is the cheap part. The expensive part is the escalation path. Any system that decides "I am confident enough to act alone" needs a second decision: "I am not, send this to a human." The quality of that second decision decides whether the product is safe. Reporting on the pilot notes that the real escalation rate in production is still unclear. That is the number I would ask for before any other.

Second, a sandbox waives enforcement, not physics. The agreement can relax state rules for a company that follows its contract. It cannot make a bad refill good. Whatever safety case exists has to live in the system itself: the drug allowlist, the data checks, the logging, the stop conditions.

Third, the allowlist is the most honest design decision in the whole thing. Roughly 190 drugs, no controlled substances, no new prescriptions, no treatment changes. That is a narrow action space. In my experience, narrowing the action space is the single most reliable way to make an AI system trustworthy. Most failed LLM products I have seen tried to do everything on day one.

Fourth, auditability is not optional. If a refill goes wrong, someone needs to reconstruct exactly what the system saw, what it checked, and why it decided. That means an immutable decision log with the inputs, not a chat transcript. I build with the assumption that every automated decision will be examined later by someone who was not in the room.

Fifth, and this is my bias showing: where the patient data goes matters. A pipeline that ships sensitive records to a remote model for every decision has a bigger attack surface and a harder compliance story than one that does the verification step close to the data. For anything touching health records, I would push as much of the checking as possible on-device or inside the provider's own boundary, and send out only what is strictly needed.

None of this means the pilot is wrong. A supervised, narrow, time-boxed experiment is exactly how a high-stakes capability should be tested. My worry is the other direction: that the headline becomes "AI can prescribe" and the metrics that matter, escalation rate, adverse events, where liability sits, stay invisible.

If you are building anything similar in any regulated field, here is a checklist I would hold myself to:

Define the action space as narrowly as you can stand.
Measure and publish how often the system defers to a human.
Log every decision with its inputs so it can be replayed.
Keep sensitive data inside the smallest boundary that works.
Decide in advance what number makes you shut it off.

Autonomy is not a model capability. It is a promise about what happens when the model is wrong.

The teams that earn trust in regulated AI will be the ones who publish their deferral rate first.

title: Anthropic says open models carry "more risk." It depends on whose risk you count.
body:
Here is what is reported. At the International AI Summit in Dublin on October 14, Anthropic executive Guillaume Princen said open alternatives to closed models carry more risk of cybersecurity incidents and other dangers. His words, as quoted: "I can't talk for open models. But by definition, there's more risk with them." Bloomberg and Business Standard both carried the story, and Business Standard says his concern comes from Anthropic's work securing its own products.

That is the news. Here is my opinion: the statement is true in a narrow sense and misleading in the way it will be used.

Open weights do change the threat model. Once weights are public, the publisher cannot revoke access, patch a misuse pattern server-side, or watch what people ask. A hosted API gives you all three. If your only question is "who can stop a bad actor", the closed model wins that argument by construction.

But that is not the question most of my work has been about.

In the deployments I have worked on, including a defence deployment and an automotive one, the risk that kept people up at night was not a stranger misusing a model. It was the data leaving the building. When the input is sensor footage, or customer conversations, or anything an auditor will ask about, "send it to someone else's server and trust their controls" is the riskiest design on the table. Not the safest.

So "more risk" depends on whose risk you count. The vendor counts the risk of the model being misused. The operator counts the risk of the data being exposed, the service being switched off, or the terms changing on a Tuesday. Those are different ledgers, and a summit stage tends to show only one of them.

My bias is no secret. Models should run where the data is: on-device, offline, under your control. That is not ideology. It is what we had to do for an offline multilingual avatar that had to work with no network at all, and for detection systems that could not wait on a round trip. Open weights are what made that possible. A closed API was never an option there.

I also do not want to wave away the concern, because part of it is real. Open weights mean the safety work shipped with the model can be fine-tuned away. Anyone running one in production inherits the job of guardrails, evaluation, and monitoring. In my experience most teams underestimate that job. They download a checkpoint, see good demo output, and ship it with none of the controls a hosted provider would have run for them.

That is the honest version of the argument. Open models do not carry more risk by definition. They move the risk from the vendor to you. If you are not set up to carry it, you should not be running one.

What would a fair comparison look like? I would want to see it measured, not asserted. Incidents per deployment, split by closed API and self-hosted. Data-exposure events counted alongside misuse events. Nobody I know has published that, and until someone does, "by definition" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Here is the checklist I would apply before choosing either side:

1. Where does the data have to live, and who is allowed to see it?
2. What happens to the product if the vendor changes pricing, policy, or availability?
3. Who owns evaluation and abuse monitoring after launch?
4. Can you reproduce a result a year from now, with the exact model you used today?

Closed models answer the third question for you and fail the second and fourth. Open models answer the second and fourth and hand you the third. Neither is free.

The vendors have a real interest in this debate, and so do I. Read every claim about "risk" with that in mind, mine included.

The takeaway: open weights do not make a system riskier by definition. They make you the one responsible for the risk, and that is a feature only if you are ready for it.

title: Meta's 816B open model needs 700 GB of memory. Open weights is not on-device.
body:
Meta just released the weights of an 816-billion-parameter model, and the minimum memory to run it is around 700 GB. "Open" and "runs where your data is" are not the same sentence.

Here is what is reported. On October 15, Meta published Muse Spark Open on Hugging Face. It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model: 816B total parameters, 42B active per token, a 1M-token context window, built for coding and long-horizon agent work. Weights ship in BF16 and NVFP4. It is also listed on Amazon SageMaker, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry. Bloomberg covered the release, and the Hugging Face model card and Meta's own research post confirm the specs.

The part most headlines skip: the model card recommends at least 700 GB of VRAM for the NVFP4 version and about 2 TB for BF16. Community reports of running it on a pair of high-end Mac Studios are impressive, and also tell you what the floor looks like.

I have spent years pushing one bias: models should run where the data is. On-device, offline, under your control. The offline multilingual avatar I built for an automotive client had to work with no network at all. A defence deployment I worked on could not send a single frame off the box. In both cases the model size was a design constraint, not a bragging number.

By that standard, 42B active parameters is a compute story. 816B total is a memory story. Active parameters set your cost per token. Total parameters set whether you can host the thing at all. Everyone quotes the first number because it is smaller.

So who actually benefits from this release? Mostly organisations that can rent or own a multi-hundred-gigabyte GPU node. That is a real group: a bank, a hospital network, a government lab that cannot ship data to a third-party API. For them, weights in hand beat an API. They can audit, fine-tune, pin a version, and keep the inference inside their own perimeter.

For a startup with one GPU, nothing changes. You will still reach this model through a hosted provider, and at that point you have traded one dependency for another, with a nicer license file.

Speaking of the license: it is not a standard open-source license. Meta calls it the Muse Model License. It permits use, fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution, but model-as-a-service providers above 20 million dollars in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Meta. That is a reasonable commercial line. It is also not what most engineers mean by open source, and procurement teams should read it before anyone builds on it.

What I would do with this release if I were evaluating it this week:

First, measure on your own task, not the leaderboard. A coding-agent benchmark tells you little about your document pipeline or your Indic-language workload. I have watched strong general models hallucinate badly in Indic languages, and no headline score showed it.

Second, test the quantized build, not the BF16 one. If NVFP4 loses accuracy on your data, the whole on-prem story changes.

Third, price total memory, not active parameters. Budget the node, the networking, the failure case and the person who gets paged.

Fourth, ask what the smaller sibling does. In production, I rarely need the biggest model. I need the smallest one that clears my error budget, and a distilled version of a model like this may be where the real value lands.

None of this makes the release unimportant. A US lab shipping frontier-scale weights that anyone can download, inspect and fine-tune is good for the ecosystem. More eyes on a model means more honest evaluation.

But "open weights" is a licensing fact. "Runs where your data is" is an engineering fact. Do not let the first one convince you the second one is solved.

Takeaway: before you celebrate an open model, divide your available memory by its total parameters, not its active ones.

title: Eight states sued OpenAI over the word "safe." Can you prove yours?
body:
Eight US states just sued OpenAI over one word: "safe."

Here is what is reported. On October 14, attorneys general from Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia filed separate suits under their own consumer protection laws. The allegation, as reported by The Hill and Al Jazeera, is that OpenAI misled users about how safe ChatGPT is, with a focus on children. The complaints cite dangerous medical advice and content touching on self-harm and violence. The states want penalties and changes to company practices. OpenAI's response was that no system is perfect and that it will keep working with experts, pointing to parental controls and break reminders.

These are allegations. Nothing has been decided, and I am not going to pretend to know who wins.

Here is my opinion: this is a consumer protection case, and consumer protection law asks a boring question. Can you show your work?

"Safe" is a marketing word. In a courtroom it becomes a claim, and a claim needs evidence. What was the test set? How was it built? What failure rate did you measure, on which kinds of users, and what did you do when the number was bad? If the honest answer is "we ran some red-team sessions before launch," that is not a safety case. That is a story about a safety case.

I have shipped AI systems in settings where "it usually works" was never an acceptable answer, including a defence deployment where a wrong output had real consequences. The discipline in those projects was not clever. Define the failure modes in writing. Build an evaluation set that actually contains the bad cases. Measure on every release. Keep the numbers. Decide in advance what result blocks a launch.

That last part is the one most teams skip. A threshold you set after seeing the result is not a threshold.

My own research on hallucination, especially in Indic languages, points at the same gap. A model can look fine in English and fail quietly in Hindi or Kannada, and nobody notices because nobody measured. Averages hide the users who get hurt. If your safety claim is one global number, you have not yet looked at the people it fails.

This is why I keep building evaluation tooling as open packages, such as hallucination-detector and model-drift-detector, rather than treating it as an afterthought. Safety is a measurement problem before it is a policy problem.

There is also an architecture angle. When a model runs where the data is, on-device or inside an organisation's own boundary, the deployer owns the evaluation, the logs and the guardrails. When you ship a general chatbot to everyone, you inherit every context at once, from a teenager at midnight to a patient asking about dosage. You cannot test for a population you cannot define. Narrow deployments are easier to certify honestly.

If you build with LLMs, here is what I would do this week:

First, write down every safety claim in your product, including the ones in marketing copy and onboarding screens. Second, next to each claim, write the evidence. If the evidence column is empty, either fix the product or soften the claim.

Third, evaluate on the subgroups you actually serve: age, language, domain. A single aggregate score is not enough.

Fourth, keep an audit trail. If a regulator or a court asks what you knew and when, "we believed it was fine" will not hold up.

Whatever happens in these eight cases, the direction is clear. Safety claims are about to be treated like financial claims: you say it, you prove it, you keep the receipts.

If you cannot measure it, do not call it safe.

title: China would regulate running AI models abroad, not renting them. Know where yours run.
body:
Here is what is reported. On October 16, China's commerce ministry proposed export controls on 23 AI technologies, including those involving models, agents and computing clusters. Reuters carried it, and TBS News reported the same proposal. The ministry framed it as security-driven: prevent misuse, keep AI under human control.

The detail I care about is one line. The proposal would cover overseas deployment of restricted models. It would exclude access through APIs, websites, apps and SaaS platforms.

Read that again. Renting the model is fine. Running the model is regulated.

This is a proposal, not a rule. Details may change, and I am not a trade lawyer. But the shape of it is worth taking seriously, because it points at the thing I keep saying: where a model runs is a design decision, and it is about to become a compliance decision too.

I have spent years building systems where the model has to live next to the data. An offline multilingual avatar for an automotive client. Real-time detection in a defence deployment, where a round trip to someone else's cloud was never an option. In those projects, the model was an artifact we shipped, versioned and pinned. Nobody could change it under us, and nobody could switch it off.

An API-only architecture is the opposite. You get convenience, and you give up control. If the rules treat hosted access and local deployment differently, the two paths stop being merely technical alternatives. They carry different legal exposure.

Here is the practical problem. Most teams I see have not written down which of their dependencies are weights they run and which are endpoints they call. Ask them where a given model physically executes, and under whose terms, and you get a pause.

If a rule like this lands in any jurisdiction, three things follow:

First, your model inventory matters. You need a list of every model in production: its source, its licence, its version, and where it runs. Not in a slide, in a file under version control.

Second, portability is a risk control. If your product only works with one provider's hosted endpoint, you have a single point of failure that regulation can hit from either side. If it can swap between hosted and local models, you have options.

Third, on-device and offline stops being a niche. When someone tells me a local model is a nice-to-have, I ask what happens the day the endpoint is unavailable to them. Then it is not a nice-to-have.

None of this means local is always better. Hosted models are often stronger, and running your own means you own patching, evaluation and monitoring. I have shipped both. The honest answer is that it depends on the data, the latency budget and the failure you can least afford.

But "it depends" has to be a decision you made on purpose. Too many systems made it by default, because the API key was the fastest way to a demo.

So here is the test I would run this week. Pick your most important AI feature and answer four questions. Which model does it use? Where does that model execute? Who can change or revoke it? What is your fallback if that path closes?

If you cannot answer all four in five minutes, you do not have an architecture. You have a dependency.

Controls will come and go, and details will shift. The teams that handle it well will be the ones who already know what they are running, and where.

Know where your models run before someone else's rulebook asks.

title: Jais 3 shipped six open Arabic models. Indic languages are still waiting for the same.
body:
Here is what is reported. On October 15, MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models and Inception42 released Jais 3: six open language models from 900 million to 375 billion parameters, plus Jais Speech for Arabic and its dialects. Both are on Hugging Face. The developers say they trained on Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, and that they are publishing the audited set of 24 Arabic benchmarks alongside the models.

The headline number is a jump on their Arabic evaluations for the 7B model, from 56.4 for the base model to 79.6. That is the developers' own result, not independent testing. Treat it as a claim until someone else reproduces it.

Here is my opinion: the benchmark release matters more than the model.

When I worked on hallucination in Indic languages, the hardest part was never getting a model to produce fluent text. It was knowing how often the fluent text was wrong. A multilingual model can look fine in English and fall apart in a lower-resource language, and the usual leaderboards will not tell you.

Fluency hides failure. A confident sentence in Hindi, Kannada or Marathi reads as correct to anyone who does not check the facts. The error rate lives in the evaluation set, not in the demo.

That is why I like the way this launch is packaged. A language-native model family, a speech model, and the evaluation suite in the same release. Most regional-language efforts ship the first and skip the last.

Second point: the size range. Six models from under a billion to hundreds of billions means a team can pick the one that fits its hardware. My bias has not changed. Models should run where the data is. In the defence and education deployments I have been part of, the data could not leave the building, and a small model that speaks the local language well beats a giant one you are not allowed to call.

A 900M model that handles dialect properly can run on a modest device with no network. A model you reach through an API cannot do that, however good its benchmark.

What I would do before adopting any of these:

1. Build your own test set from real user text in your language, with dialect and code-mixing. Public benchmarks are a starting point, not a verdict.
2. Measure hallucination separately from fluency. Ask factual questions with known answers and score the wrong ones.
3. Test the smallest model first. If it clears your bar, you get on-device deployment and lower cost.
4. Check the speech path separately. A good text model with a weak speech front end is still a weak product.

India has hundreds of languages and dialects, and most of the useful text in them is not in clean web corpora. The Arabic effort shows the pattern: open weights, open checkpoints, open evaluation, and a recipe others can copy.

I would like to see the same for Indic languages, with the benchmarks published first.

Takeaway: a language model is only as trustworthy as its evaluation set, so ask for the eval before you ask for the weights.

title: Mixture-of-experts models compute like a 2B and store like a 24B. Ask about memory.
body:
Liquid AI released LFM2.5-24B-A2B on October 13. By the catalog and blog listings I could find, it is a 24B-parameter mixture-of-experts reasoning model that activates about 2B parameters per token, with a 128K context window and open weights under its own LFM Open License. The same listings put a Q4_K_M quantized build at roughly 14.5 GB.

Those are the facts that two independent sources agree on. The benchmark claims, including a comparison against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on agentic tasks, come from Liquid's own launch material. No third party had evaluated the checkpoint in what I found. Treat the scores as a vendor's claim until someone else reproduces them.

Now the part I care about. Active parameters decide how fast each token is computed. Total parameters decide how much memory you need to hold the model. A model that computes like a 2B and stores like a 24B is a very good deal on a workstation. It is a different deal on a phone, a drone, or an embedded board.

I have shipped offline systems where the hardware budget was fixed before the model was chosen. In those projects the first question was never "how smart is it". It was "does it fit in memory next to everything else the device has to run". Speed was the second question. Mixture-of-experts helps with the second and does nothing for the first.

That is why a 14.5 GB file matters more to me than the 2B figure. It tells you which class of device can hold the thing at all. A laptop with enough RAM, yes. A typical phone, no. An air-gapped edge box with a proper accelerator, probably, if you leave headroom for the context cache.

And the context cache is the other number people skip. A 128K window is a ceiling, not a free feature. On constrained hardware you will cap it far lower, and your real memory plan is weights plus cache plus the rest of your application.

There is a real step forward here, though. Routing only a few experts per token means latency and energy per token behave like a small model. For an agent that makes many short calls in a loop, that is exactly what you want. Fewer joules per step is the difference between an agent you can leave running locally and one you only demo.

The licence deserves a read as well. Open weights under a custom licence with conditions on commercial use is not the same as Apache 2.0. If you are building something for a defence or regulated client, your legal team needs to see the terms before your engineers fall in love with the benchmark chart.

So here is how I would evaluate it. First, write down the memory ceiling of the device you actually ship to. Second, subtract the OS, your application, and a realistic context cache. Third, see whether a quantized 24B fits in what is left. Only then look at the accuracy numbers, and run them on your own data, in your own language, on your own hardware.

My bias is well known: models should run where the data is, offline and under your control. Mixture-of-experts moves us closer to that. But the spec sheet number that gets quoted is the compute number, and the number that decides whether you can deploy is the memory one.

Takeaway: when someone says a model is small because it has few active parameters, ask how many gigabytes you have to load.

title: Hot take: "private AI" is a deployment fact, not a marketing sentence
body:
Apple and Google announced a multi-year deal in January under which the next generation of Apple Foundation Models will be based on Google's Gemini models and cloud technology. Apple's line is that Apple Intelligence keeps running on the device and on Private Cloud Compute, and that only the minimum data needed leaves the phone.

Here is what is still not public. Bloomberg reported the two companies were discussing hosting the chatbot on Google servers running TPUs. Reporting that followed the earnings call noted that Apple is not releasing details of the Google arrangement, and that neither company has said definitively where the Gemini-based Siri runs.

I am not here to accuse anyone. I am here to point at the gap, because I see the same gap in almost every AI project I review.

"Private" gets used to describe three very different things. One: the model weights sit on the device and no request leaves it. Two: the request leaves, but goes to infrastructure the vendor controls and says it cannot read. Three: the request goes to a partner's cloud under a contract. All three get the same word in a slide deck. Only the first is something you can verify by pulling the network cable.

In the defence and government-adjacent deployments I have worked on, that distinction was never philosophical. It decided the architecture. If the data cannot leave the building, the model has to come to the data. You then spend your time on quantisation, memory budgets, latency on modest hardware and offline updates, instead of arguing about trust.

The same was true for an offline multilingual avatar I shipped for an automotive client. The reason it worked in the real environment was boring: it did not need a connection to do its job.

Cloud-hosted models are not bad. Frontier capability is real, and for plenty of workloads a well-governed cloud call is the right trade. Apple's Private Cloud Compute is a serious attempt at making that trade defensible. My complaint is narrower: users and buyers should be told which of the three they are getting, in plain words, before they hand over a calendar, a message history or a patient record.

If you are building or buying an assistant this quarter, ask four questions and expect specific answers.

Where does inference run for the common request, and where for the hard one? What exactly leaves the device on the fallback path? Who can read it, and what is the retention? Can I get the same behaviour with the network disabled?

If the answer to the last one is "no", that is fine, but then it is a cloud product with a good privacy policy, and it should be evaluated like one.

I keep my bias in the open: models should run where the data is. On-device, offline, under your control. Not because the cloud is evil, but because the only guarantee you can audit yourself is the one that never leaves your hardware.

Takeaway: when a vendor says "private", ask where the weights run. The answer is the product.

title: Computer-use agents click buttons. Your code decides whether they should.
body:
Hot take: the scariest part of a computer-use agent is not the model. It is the thirty lines of glue code that execute whatever the model asks for.

The pattern is simple. The model looks at a screenshot and returns an action: click here, type this. A program you wrote carries it out with a browser driver or a desktop automation library. The model never touches the machine itself. OpenAI introduced this with Operator in January 2025 and added a computer use tool to its Responses API in March 2025, and Microsoft's Azure documentation describes the same split between model and developer-run integration layer.

That split is the whole security story. Everything the agent can do, your executor lets it do.

I have shipped enough systems for defence and enterprise settings to know what happens when a demo meets a real environment. The demo works on a clean page. Production has expired sessions, cookie banners, a popup that appeared for the first time on a Tuesday, and a button that says Delete next to a button that says Save.

So here is how I think about building one of these properly.

First, the executor is a policy engine, not a pipe. Every action the model proposes should pass through an allowlist: which domains, which windows, which action types. Anything outside it is refused and logged, no matter how confident the model sounds.

Second, irreversible actions need a human. Sending, paying, deleting, submitting. The agent can prepare them. A person approves them. This costs a few seconds and saves a week of incident review.

Third, log screenshots with actions. When something goes wrong you need to see what the model saw, not just what it did. Without that, debugging is guessing.

Fourth, assume the screen is untrusted input. A web page can contain text written to steer the model. If your agent reads a page and treats its contents as instructions, you have built a prompt injection channel with a mouse attached. Separate what the user asked for from what the screen says.

Fifth, test failure, not success. Run the agent against pages that are slow, broken, or lying. Measure how often it stops safely versus how often it presses on. The second number is the one that matters.

There is also a deployment question that people skip. Screenshots of your internal tools, your customer records, your dashboards are being sent somewhere to be interpreted. For a lot of the work I do, that is a non-starter. My bias is that models should run where the data is: on-device, offline, under your control. A smaller vision model running locally that handles a narrow workflow reliably beats a frontier model you cannot legally point at the screen.

None of this makes computer-use agents bad. They are genuinely useful, especially for legacy software with no API, which is most of the world's software. But the capability is arriving faster than the discipline around it.

When people ask me whether an agent is ready, I do not ask about the benchmark score. I ask what the executor refuses to do, who approves the irreversible steps, and where the screenshots go.

If you cannot answer those three questions, you do not have an agent in production. You have a demo with a mouse.

Takeaway: the model proposes, your code disposes. Build the part that says no first.

title: The EU AI Act delay is a head start, not a reprieve. Most teams will waste it.
body:
Teams I talk to are treating the EU AI Act delay like a snooze button. That is the wrong read.

The Digital Omnibus on AI is now law. High-risk obligations for Annex III systems, the ones that touch employment, credit, education and law enforcement, moved from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I moved to 2 August 2028. Two independent legal and research write-ups agree on those dates.

Here is the part that gets lost in the headlines. The transparency duties in Article 50 were not delayed. Telling people they are talking to a machine and labelling synthetic content already applies. The Commission's powers to fine providers of general-purpose models also started on 2 August 2026.

So the calendar did not get emptier. It got uneven. Some obligations are live today and some are a year or two out.

I have shipped enough systems into defence, automotive and education settings to know how this goes. The deadline is never the hard part. The hard part is that nobody can answer, on demand, what a model did, on which data, under which version, and who approved it. In a defence deployment I worked on, that question was asked in the first week of review, not the last.

If you wait for the final deadline, you will be reconstructing evidence for a system that has been running for two years. Logs that were never kept cannot be recovered. Prompts that were never versioned cannot be replayed. Evaluation sets that nobody froze cannot be compared against.

The extra time is a gift only if you spend it on the unglamorous work. Here is what I would do now:

First, version everything that shapes behaviour: model weights, system prompts, retrieval indexes, guardrail rules. If you cannot pin it, you cannot defend it.

Second, keep an evaluation set that is frozen and dated. When a regulator or a customer asks whether quality regressed, you want a number from last quarter and a number from today, produced by the same harness.

Third, log decisions at the boundary where a human or a downstream system acts on a model output. Not every token. The decision, the inputs that mattered, and the model version.

Fourth, classify your own systems honestly. Most teams I see either claim nothing is high-risk or panic that everything is. Write down the reasoning for each system, because the reasoning is what gets reviewed.

Fifth, run hallucination and drift checks continuously. This is why I built tooling for it as open packages rather than leaving it as a quarterly exercise. A check that runs on every release becomes evidence. A check that runs once becomes an anecdote.

There is also an architectural angle that I keep coming back to. The easier it is to keep a model, its data and its logs inside a boundary you control, the easier every one of these obligations becomes. When inference runs on-device or on your own infrastructure, you can answer where the data went with one sentence. When it runs through three vendors, you need three contracts and a diagram.

None of this is exciting. That is the point. Compliance work rewards the teams that were already disciplined about engineering, and punishes the ones who treated governance as a document to write at the end.

A delayed deadline is not a cancelled one. Use the extra year to build the evidence trail, because the system you ship today is the one you will be asked to explain in 2027.

title: Sovereign AI starts with weights you can actually run, and Kolibri makes that harder to dodge
body:
Sovereign AI starts with a weights file you can actually run, and Kolibri just made that argument harder to dodge.

On October 3, Aleph Alpha released Kolibri, a German-English mixture-of-experts model, as open weights under Apache 2.0. The model card lists roughly 78B total parameters and about 3.5B active per token. It was trained from scratch on infrastructure in Germany and Finland. Both the Hugging Face card and independent write-ups agree on those numbers.

I care about this for a reason that has nothing to do with benchmarks. My bias has always been that models should run where the data is: on-device, offline, under your control. Every defence and enterprise deployment I have worked on started with the same question. Where is the data allowed to go? Usually the answer was "nowhere".

In that world, an API is not an option, however good the model behind it. A permissive licence plus downloadable weights is the entry ticket. Without it, the conversation ends before it begins.

But here is where I want to be honest, because the sovereignty pitch tends to skip this part. Open weights are not the same as easy to run. Reports put the deployment floor at about two H100 80GB cards or one H200. That is not a laptop, and it is not an edge box in a field unit. It is a proper server you have to buy, power, cool and patrol.

The active-parameter count makes compute per token look small. Memory is what you pay for. All the experts have to be resident, so you are provisioning for 78B even though each token touches a fraction of that. I see teams get this wrong constantly when they size hardware from the headline number.

Then there is the evidence. The benchmark claims around Kolibri are mostly from the vendor and community write-ups. I have not seen independent evaluation, and I would not put a number in a procurement document on that basis. When I evaluate a model for a regulated deployment, I run it on the customer's own data and the customer's own failure cases. A leaderboard score tells me nothing about how the model behaves on a noisy scanned form or a mixed-language query.

Language coverage is the other thing I look at first. A German-English model is a real win for European regulated industries. It also makes me think about the languages that keep waiting. In my own research on hallucination in Indic languages, the gap between a well-supported language and a thinly supported one was the main finding, not a footnote. A sovereign model for one region does not become a sovereign model for another.

So what would I do with Kolibri if I were scoping a project tomorrow?

First, I would pull the weights and run them on one box inside the target network, with no outbound calls. If that single step cannot happen, the project has a sovereignty problem regardless of the licence.

Second, I would measure memory and latency at the context lengths we really need. The card allows over a million tokens but recommends staying at or below about 262K for serving. Most real workloads need a small fraction of that, and I would size for that fraction.

Third, I would build an evaluation set from the customer's data before making any quality promise. Retrieval quality and hallucination rates on their documents decide whether the system ships, not the model's reported maths score.

Fourth, I would ask whether a much smaller model does the job. Most production systems I have built did not need a frontier-class model. They needed a reliable one, close to the data.

Open weights from European labs are a healthy development. They give regulated teams a real option, and they put pressure on closed vendors to justify what they charge for sending your data elsewhere.

The takeaway: sovereignty is not a licence, it is a deployment you can run, size and audit yourself. Download the weights, put them on your own hardware, and test them on your own data before you believe anyone's slide.

title: Hot take: a frontier model behind a staged rollout is a preview, not infrastructure
body:
Hot take: a frontier model you can only get through a staged rollout is not infrastructure. It is a preview.

Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30. Its own post pitches it at complex software engineering, knowledge work and cybersecurity defense, with a 1M token output limit. It also says Google is prioritising safety and testing before a wider public release, and access began with trusted testers. Independent coverage from 9to5Google and others confirms the same pattern: the model is real, the access is gated, and reports disagree on how broad that access is today.

I am not criticising the staged rollout. Careful release is the right call for a model pitched at finding and patching vulnerabilities. I am pointing at what it means for anyone building on top.
